2.4.1.5-f15.accuracy_reason: Syrupus de pomis regis Sabor (King Sapor's syrup of apples) was a standard syrup in Mesue's tradition.

2.4.1.5-f16.accuracy_reason: Diamargaritum is a pearl electuary, and 'calidum' and 'frigidum' are its humoral hot and cold forms, both listed in the passage.

2.4.1.5-f2.accuracy_reason: Burton completes the scholastic maxim 'frustra fit per plura quod fieri potest per pauciora' after '(as the saying is)', and it is a form of the principle of economy.

2.4.1.5-f23.accuracy_reason: The note says there was a single formula attributed to both Galen and Rhazes. Period pharmacopoeias list two separate confections, an electuarium laetificans Galeni and one Rhasis, and Burton is naming both.

2.4.1.5-f25.accuracy_reason: Unguentum populeum was indeed a cooling, soporific ointment of poplar buds with poppy, mandrake, henbane and similar herbs.

2.4.1.5-f26.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.7, describes Chaos as 'rudis indigestaque moles'.

2.4.1.5-f35.accuracy_reason: Diatrion pipereon was the confection of the three peppers: black, white and long.

2.4.1.5-f40.accuracy_reason: The Pharmacopoeia Londinensis was issued in 1618.

2.4.1.5-f7.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.2.14, reads 'quidquid delirant reges plectuntur Achivi'; Burton does leave out 'quidquid'.

2.4.1.5-f9.accuracy_reason: Horace, Ars Poetica 70–72, has 'cadentque quae nunc sunt in honore vocabula, si volet usus'; the note quotes it correctly.
